title: Infant Formula, Powder, Non-Soy
lede: The most directly scoped pilot evidence is a US survey of cow-milk powdered formula. Its results are reported as prepared for feeding, so they cannot be compared directly with limits for powder as sold.

scope.geography_market: Source-specific US datasets and EU reference context; not a worldwide estimate
scope.period: Historical source periods as stated; pilot assembled 2026-10-17
scope.population_route: Infants consuming formula; oral route; no feeding change recommendation
scope.comparator_outcome: Occurrence, source-specific interventions and decision requirements; not certification
scope.analytes: tAs, Pb, Cd and tHg in direct FDA survey; other metals/species not assessed as a complete body
scope.material_form: Non-soy infant formula powder; direct survey evidence limited to cow-milk powder
scope.basis: Prepared for feeding in FDA survey; as-sold powder kept separate for legal examples
scope.stage: Inputs, manufacturing, powder as sold, preparation and ingestion

answers.text: This page concerns non-soy infant formula sold as powder. The direct survey subset is specifically cow-milk-based powder. The broader category must not imply that every non-soy formulation was sampled.

Soy powder, ready-to-feed liquid, concentrated liquid and amino-acid formula remain separate evidence scopes. Powder as sold and formula prepared for feeding also require separate values, even when they describe the same product.

Infants are the intended users and ingestion is the relevant route. Specialty indications, follow-on use and other age groups require explicit classification. This evidence page does not recommend changing an infant's feeding or dilution instructions.

The FDA survey measured total arsenic, lead, cadmium and total mercury in the cow-milk powder subset. Detection establishes occurrence under the source's analytical method; it does not by itself establish a health effect or noncompliance.

Manufacturers should retain input traceability and powder/prepared-basis records; buyers should request matched lot evidence. The survey supports analyte-specific investigation, not selection of a universally clean brand or the attribution of contamination to one ingredient.

Current market representativeness, brand-to-brand variance, ingredient apportionment and evaluated control effectiveness remain unresolved here. A category table cannot predict an untested lot or establish an individual infant's exposure.

The directly matched FDA label is cow-milk-based powdered formula, tested during FY2023–FY2025. The table is recalculated from the existing sample/analyte records; related liquid, soy and amino-acid groups are excluded from these counts.

There are 230 cow-milk powder samples per analyte. Counts of numerical results, censored results and observed maxima remain separate. The same products measured for four analytes are not 920 independent products.

This special survey is not treated as market-share-weighted surveillance. Broader formula studies remain in the source index but are not merged without resolving formulation, format, preparation and overlap. Sample maxima are not population maxima. In the cow-milk powder subset, the calculated sample median for total arsenic is 0.2 µg/kg in FY2023 (29 samples) and 0.4 µg/kg in FY2025 (126 samples), using conservative censoring bounds. Different sampled products and counts prevent this sample-level difference from establishing a market-wide trend. No collection-region labels are supplied in the source table.

Milk-derived ingredients, other recipe inputs, water and mineral premixes are investigation targets. The selected finished-product survey does not measure their individual contributions; it cannot rank ingredients as proven contamination drivers.

Equipment contact, handling and packaging are plausible investigation stages, but the selected evidence does not apportion finished-product metal levels to them. A contact-material result would need relevant food, contact conditions and migration evidence.

Formulation and ingredient origins change what must be measured. A composition model can generate a hypothesis only when input concentrations, inclusion rates, yields and preparation are known. The old ingredient-driver estimates are not retained as measured attribution.

FDA converted as-sold analyses to prepared-for-feeding values using each label. This changes the reporting basis; it does not demonstrate removal during manufacturing. No universal powder-to-liquid conversion factor is used.

The pilot has not established equipment or packaging migration rates for this exact formula scope. Bulk metal content of a container is not the amount migrating into formula. Direct contact testing is needed for that claim.
Effects of storage time, temperature and preparation conditions have not been assessed as a body of evidence here. No storage-related reduction or increase is assumed from the occurrence survey.

An exposure calculation needs consumed formula amount, preparation, frequency and body weight. FDA's reported preparation conversion assumes no metal contribution from water; an actual-use estimate must examine that assumption for its water source.

The population is infants, but this survey does not measure individual feeding patterns or infant health outcomes. High-consumption scenarios require suitable intake data and an explicit age and body-weight distribution.

An exposure estimate describes intake under its assumptions. It is not a diagnosis, a measured health outcome or proof of causation. Changing preparation dilution is not presented as a contamination-control option.

No comparative intervention review for this exact formula category has been completed in this pilot. The operational controls below are proposed verification steps, not quantified claims that a process reduces metal content.

Effect sizes, nutrient trade-offs, process safety, cost and commercial implementation need direct evaluation. Ingredient substitution cannot be ranked only by metal concentration; formulation and nutritional constraints need separate assessment.

Supplier qualification can prevent entry of unsuitable material; testing detects; rejection excludes a lot. None is evidence of chemical removal. Blending or reconstitution changes concentration and must not be presented as metal removal or a validated mitigation method.

answers.text: Separate manufacturing-lot release, supplier surveillance and process validation. Identify lots, increments, independent products and composites. The FDA survey's sample count does not prescribe the number of tests needed to release a production lot.

FDA used ICP-MS for the reported total-element analyses. Inorganic arsenic, methylmercury and Cr(VI) require appropriate species-specific methods; total-element values cannot substitute for those species. Preserve preparation, method limits and uncertainty.

A COA applies to the identified sample and analytes. Buyers need traceability to the delivered lot, sampling coverage and method suitability. A historical category mean, a single negative result or an unmatched COA cannot characterize all production.

Manufacturers should obtain material identity, supplier and lot traceability, analytical basis, relevant contaminant results and change notifications. Packaging claims require contact-condition evidence. These requirements support an investigation; they are not measured benefits from the survey.

Retailers should request the actual product scope, tested lots, laboratory methods, reporting limits, preparation basis and evidence supporting claimed reductions. Counsel should retain primary reports, dated instruments and correction history rather than rely on a generic safe/unsafe label.

Investigate material substitutions, new suppliers, process/contact changes, preparation-label changes, anomalous results and revised requirements. Reassess the affected scope and use a documented release or escalation decision rather than extrapolate the previous survey.

The table gives dated EU primary-instrument examples for lead and cadmium in powder as placed on the market. It is an illustration of matching requirements, not a complete current legal opinion for every market or every non-soy formulation.

The displayed FDA results are prepared-for-feeding values; these EU examples are as-sold powder limits. A direct ratio or pass/fail comparison is invalid. Matching requires the actual preparation conversion and the applicable analytical decision rule.

Other analytes, species and markets have not been verified to completion here. This is unresolved applicability, not a claim that no government regulates them. Certification read-across values are not substituted for a government requirement.

Primary text: Regulation (EU) 2023/915, consolidation of 1 July 2025, inspected 17 October 2026. These are dated examples of binding food maximum levels; amendments after that consolidation and current transaction applicability remain to be checked. No certification limits are changed. [[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels]]

answers.text: This pilot has not completed an authoritative search of metal-related recalls and enforcement for this category. No event is presented as verified, and the section does not claim that no events exist.

An event record must identify the product and lots, date, authority, contaminant, primary notice, action status and later corrections. Allegations, voluntary actions and final findings need separate labels. Existing unsourced category statements are not retained as established events.
A verified event would apply first to its identified product and time. It cannot establish the prevalence of contamination across all non-soy formula, nor the condition of current production.

This is a selected-existing-corpus pilot, with reproducible filtering of the FDA survey and an inventory of legacy linked sources. The full formula literature and public-event registers have not been systematically searched and screened for these questions.

Exact cow-milk powder rows support the occurrence table. Other formulation or format rows are contextual until their scope is resolved. Ingredient findings do not become finished-formula values, and overlapping reports must not count as independent studies.

The assessment was updated on 18 October 2026 with survey-year comparisons. Source-wide prepared-for-feeding LOD maxima conservatively bound non-detects; individual LODs are not invented. Cross-basis compliance comparisons, modelled ingredient attribution and public standards arithmetic remain excluded.
